analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal justice grants to states that let private probation companies charge fees to people jailed for unpaid fines.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the House before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Some states and counties let private companies supervise people placed on probation only because they could not pay a court fine or fee, and those companies charge the probationer their own monthly fees on top. This bill would deny those states and localities federal Edward Byrne Justice Assistance Grant money if they kept such contracts, and would require annual public reporting of every private probation contract and what the contractors charge. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Poor people who owe court fines and fees. In states that kept the contracts, they would no longer face a private company adding its own monthly fees to a debt they already could not pay, and would no longer risk jail or extended probation just for being unable to pay. Taxpayers also gain transparency through the required annual list of private probation contracts and payments [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People jailed or fined for being poor

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funds from going to any state or local government with a contract under which a company collects court fines from a pay-only probationer and charges that probationer a fee for the collection [S3].

It requires states to report annually, for each unit of local government, a list of private probation contractors, the amount payable to each, and whether the contractor charged a fee to a pay-only probationer [S3].
A pay-only probationer is defined as someone placed on probation solely for failing to pay a fine or fee imposed by a state or local court — not for any other offense [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private probation companies would lose a profitable line of business in any state that chose to keep the contracts rather than the grant money. States and localities would face a choice: end fee-charging probation contracts or forfeit federal justice grant funds. No other party is required to pay anything.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private probation companies and their government clients

drawbacks.text: The bill's remedy cuts federal grant money from the state or local government, not from the private company directly, so a locality that values the contract more than the grant could keep the arrangement and simply lose federal funds [S3].
Local governments that rely on court fines and fees for revenue could see those collections shrink, which some would argue leaves a funding hole that must be made up elsewhere [S3].
The condition applies only to the Byrne grant program, so a state could keep fee-charging probation contracts and lose only this stream of funding, limiting the bill's reach [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a narrow but sharply harmful practice: jailing or extending probation over unpaid fines and letting private companies add fees to that debt. The cost is real but limited — some localities would lose or have to weigh federal grant money against contractor revenue. The main honest criticism is that it polices the practice indirectly, through funding conditions rather than an outright ban.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the bill on March 24, 2017, joined at introduction by eight other House Democrats [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
On April 6, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations, and no further action appears in the record [S5].
It finished with 12 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never received a committee or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private probation companies keep collecting fees from people on probation for unpaid fines, and no locality lost any federal grant money. People stuck in pay-only probation remain in the same position.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private probation companies keep their fees

industries.note: These firms are hired by courts to supervise people on probation and charge them monthly fees for the supervision, including people on probation only for unpaid fines. The bill would cut off federal grant money to any government keeping such contracts, threatening a revenue stream built on charging the poorest probationers [S3].

industries.industry: State and local governments reliant on court fines and fees
industries.note: They would face a choice between ending fee-charging probation contracts and forfeiting Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds. Those that kept contracts would lose federal money; those that ended them would lose fine-collection arrangements but retain grants [S3].
